title: What Hera Can Learn From the Asteroid DART Hit
excerpt: DART proved a spacecraft can nudge an asteroid. It did not say how much Dimorphos weighs, what it is made of, or what the impact did to it. ESA's Hera was sent to measure it, and ESA says Hera's first detailed images are due November 25.
content:
On November 25, 2026, ESA says it will unveil Hera’s first detailed images of Dimorphos, the small asteroid NASA’s DART spacecraft hit four years ago. The date comes from an ESA announcement published on October 27, 2026. If it holds, the pictures will be the first close views of Dimorphos since the LICIACube cubesat photographed the debris in 2022.

The reason this needs a second spacecraft is a gap in what DART could tell us. DART showed that hitting an asteroid at high speed changes its orbit. It could not weigh the target, look inside it, or map the surface the impact left behind. Without those numbers, a planetary defense plan has a result but no way of knowing how far the result carries over to a different asteroid.

33 min 15 s

Shorter orbit for Dimorphos

A 2024 NASA model of the binary system after DART's impact. How it was achieved, and for how long, is what Hera measures.

What DART did and did not settle

DART struck Dimorphos on September 26, 2022, at 23:14:24 UTC. NASA’s impact-site analysis puts the spacecraft’s mass at the time at 579.4 kg and its speed at 6.1449 km/s. KeepTrack’s catalog, which carries DART as NORAD 49497 with a September 26, 2022 decay date, lists it at 610 kg at launch, so the two numbers describe different moments. It launched on a Falcon 9 from Vandenberg’s Space Launch Complex 4E on November 24, 2021, per the launch record, alongside the LICIACube cubesat that watched the aftermath.

The headline result was the change in Dimorphos’s orbit around its larger partner Didymos. A 2024 NASA study put the reduction at 33 minutes and 15 seconds, and placed Dimorphos at a mean distance of about 1,152 m from Didymos after impact, roughly 37 m closer. The same study inferred that Dimorphos now has an elongated, ellipsoidal shape. That is a model result from the orbit data, not a picture.

A second result came in March 2026. NASA reported that DART changed the pair’s orbital period around the Sun by 0.15 seconds. That is separate from the 33-minute change in how Dimorphos circles Didymos, and a much smaller number. NASA noted that Didymos was not on an impact trajectory with Earth and that DART could not have put it on one.

Our account of the impact night covers the navigation and the first results. This article is about what is still unknown.

The number everyone quotes, and why it moved

The most repeated figure from DART is the momentum enhancement. It measures how much more push the asteroid received than the spacecraft’s own momentum alone would give, because debris thrown out of the crater pushes back. The early estimate of about 3.6, reported in December 2022, assumed Didymos and Dimorphos have the same density. By March 2023, NASA gave a range of 2.2 to 4.9, depending on Dimorphos’s mass. In March 2026, NASA’s account said the factor for the impact was about two.

NASA’s summaries do not say whether the March 2026 figure rests on the same assumptions as the earlier two, so this article does not treat any one number as the final answer. What the range shows is the problem: an asteroid’s mass is the thing you need to turn an orbit change into a momentum number, and DART could not measure it.

That is Hera’s first job. ESA’s spacecraft carries 12 instruments across the main spacecraft and its two CubeSats. Its laser rangefinder works from 10 m to 20 km. Radio links between Hera and the CubeSats, with a maximum range of 60 km, let engineers watch how the small spacecraft move under the asteroids’ gravity and from that infer the mass of both.

What ESA’s announced images can show

ESA’s October 27 announcement says Hera has already seen Didymos and Dimorphos as two separate bodies, from 1,280 km. Mission manager Ian Carnelli said there that the views will grow sharper as Hera comes closer. JAXA’s operations plan of November 2 schedules the start of early characterization at 20 to 30 km on November 4, Japan time. That plan was written before the milestone, and this article does not report whether it was met. ESA’s Hera pages are the place to check.

Simulations published by ESA in 2024 predicted that Hera will probably not find a clear crater. In that modelling, about 8% of Dimorphos’s mass was shifted around its body, which would leave a reshaped asteroid rather than a pit in an otherwise intact one. The pictures can begin to separate a local crater from wholesale reshaping, but one image set will not settle what is inside.

A published simulation is a prediction, not a finding. Whether the images show a crater or none, the outcome tests the model.

The instruments behind the answer

Images show the surface. The interior needs other tools, and the CubeSats carry them.

ESA says both CubeSats will end their missions by touching down on Dimorphos. JAXA’s November 2 plan lists both deployments as still to come, so a touchdown is a plan, not a result.

Why this matters beyond one asteroid

If NASA or ESA ever had to deflect an asteroid that threatened Earth, the planners would not have DART’s luxury of a harmless target and plenty of time. They would need to predict the outcome from a model. Models need a target’s mass, strength and structure. Hera’s mission is to measure those for Dimorphos, then compare the results with what the models predicted.

For KeepTrack readers, the tracking is partly a bookkeeping question. Hera is carried in the catalog as NORAD 61449, launched on October 7, 2024 at 14:52 UTC on a Falcon 9 from Cape Canaveral LC-40, the same launch record that lists the Juventas and Milani CubeSats. The catalog shows a 1,081 kg launch mass and no Earth-orbit element set. The tracker can say what was launched, and ESA’s pages are the place to follow where it is.

For another deep look at how space agencies study asteroids close up, see our piece on the sample return era.

When will ESA release the first detailed Hera images of Dimorphos?

ESA announced on October 27, 2026 that it will unveil them on November 25, 2026.

How much did DART change Dimorphos's orbit?

A 2024 NASA study found Dimorphos's orbital period around Didymos was 33 minutes and 15 seconds shorter after the September 26, 2022 impact.

Why send Hera if DART worked?

Researchers still need Dimorphos's mass, structure and composition to interpret the impact and apply the result to another asteroid.

Will Hera see a crater from the DART impact?

ESA's 2024 simulations predicted Hera will probably not find any crater, because the impact may have reshaped the asteroid. Hera's images will test that prediction.

Was DART an emergency mission?

No. NASA says Didymos was not on an impact trajectory with Earth and that DART could not have put it on one.

When do Hera's CubeSats deploy?

JAXA's operations plan of November 2, 2026 schedules deployment from January 13 to February 2, 2027, Japan time. Dates can change.
